items.title: True grit specialists primed to challenge the run of road pro rainbow jerseys – Analysing the Gravel World Championships contenders
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
The 2026 UCI Gravel World Championships casts a spotlight on Western Australia this weekend, the first time the race for rainbows has ventured outside Europe. The rugged territory around Nannup is quite opposite, geographically and literally, of Classics-style races held across four previous editions.

There was a buzz among the dedicated off-road riders when organisers announced a course that would be dictated by wide, hard-paced dirt roads and cross rugged forests. Maybe this was the year most suited to a gravel rider, rather than another ride for WorldTour pros. The table was set, now who would commit to long-distance travel to enjoy the feast?

The cost and time to travel to Western Australia has kept some away this year and the quantity of riders will be lower this year in the elite fields but that also means that those who are making the trip are doing so with intent, rather than making a last minute decision to work it into their schedule for a day.

There's also nearly triple the amount of climbing as compared to last year in the Netherlands, the women's 125.5km contest going from 1,190 metres of elevation gain to 3,179 metres. The elite men will cover 144km with a similar bump in climbing that now totals 3,713 metres. And don't forget about the technical descents.

However, there is no lack of quality for the elite fields, most of the riders well versed in the unpredictable off-road races provided by UCI Gravel World Series, Gravel Earth Series and Life Time Grand Prix, among the leading collectives.

Two of the top riders from the Life Time Grand Prix return to the Worlds for gravel - Keegan Swenson (USA) and Sofia Gomez Villafane (Argentina) - having passed on races in Belgium and the Netherlands the last two years. Mountain bike and gravel specialist Matt Beers (South Africa) returns for the first time since 2022. The overall winners of the Gravel Earth Series are also in the lineups, Geerike Schreurs for the Netherlands, and Mads Wurtz Schmidt (Denmark).

Also back in action are last year's winner Florian Vermeersch (Belgium), and 2024 gravel world champion Marianne Vos (Netherlands), both who have been on the podium multiple times.

The home charge of six Australian women will include Oceania gravel champion Nicole Frain and gravel national champion Tiffany Cromwell, kicking up the gravel on Saturday morning. There are 11 Aussie men for their Sunday race, led by gravel national champion Cameron Scott, and 2025 national champion and SEVEN winner Mark O'Brien.

Here's a look at some of the versatile riders who are expected to make the right moves and turn the dirt roads into gold.

From the moment the name Sofia Gomez Villafañe popped up as a confirmed starter, it was hard to imagine that anyone who would enter could knock her far from the top of the favourites list. It's not that she has a stunning history at this event specifically – although she did finish a more-than-respectable 12th at the first edition in 2022 and came 34th when she last raced in 2023 – but her record outside the UCI-sanctioned domain is something to behold. The Argentinian-born rider has won Unbound Gravel 200 and The Traka 200 twice and claimed the Life Time Grand Prix series three times. It took more than half a season for her gravel winning streak to be disrupted this season.

It's understandable, however, that the UCI Gravel World Championships hasn't been high on her priority list in recent years between a Life Time Grand Prix Series clash, terrain that certainly didn't play into her hands, and a field packed with road riders that would be positioned near the front of the grid. Villafañe's haul of non-UCI wins may be heavy in gravel prestige but only gave her minimal UCI points and therefore poor positioning. Still, she did gather 200 points this year some from her win at Castellón, which is part of the UCI Gravel World Series.

Even with only a small number of points to soften the start situation it looks to be a World Gravel Championships that will play to the strengths of the top gravel specialists, with more gravel than ever before and an unrelenting series of challenging climbs. She may not start at the front of the field, but there is every chance in Nannup that is where she will end up. (SG)

A former champion on the start line of a World Championship always deserves respect, but that goes tenfold for one named Marianne Vos.

With 13 other world titles to her name, a second at this event last year along with her win in 2024, there is no question that the Dutch rider heads to the start line in Western Australia with a considerable claim on a favourite slot. What's more, her talent across the disciplines is a real asset when it comes to the large gravel World Championships fields, where road tactics can come into play as well as the skills to handle the sometimes tricky terrain. Vos has both the bike-handling skills, knowledge, experience and comfort in the field to conserve energy when she needs it most. What's more, she is one of the few international riders that will also be in familiar territory, having once been a regular at the Tour of Margaret River which ran in the area.

Add to that the unrelentingly competitive nature of the Dutch superstar in the discipline, and you can be sure she is hankering for a win after a season where they have been thin on the ground. If she comes to the finish line in a reduced group, she'll be hard to beat so her rivals are bound to work hard to drop her on the climbs before. (SG)

Since totally committing to gravel at the start of last season, Nicole Frain has made clear just how capable she is in the off-road discipline. The 2022 Australian road champion has combined her skills developed in the peloton with an ability to ride in the 'grey zone' and keep pushing hard through the race to find ample success. In fact she finished at the very top of the UCI Gravel World Series overall in 2025 and this year has captured the Oceania Championships and four UCI Gravel World Series race wins. She was 26th in the Gravel World Championships last year but it wasn't really a course that played to her strengths.

This year's addition of more gravel and climbing will suit Frain, however the extent of it could push her to the limits of her ascending abilities. Still, not surprisingly – given it is a home World Championships for Frain – she has put a target on the event and has been tracking along well in training towards it, despite a nasty bout of the flu along the way. Plus she is well aware of what she is in for having carved out the time to do a course reconnaissance earlier this year.

Her road background works in her favour to help her manage the ebb and flow of the more peloton-driven dynamic that is usually surfaces more heavily at the race than many other gravel events, but despite that her emphasis on developing the technical skills and gravel focus will give her another advantage. On top of that, she will be lining up right near the front, given she's sitting just one spot away from the top of the UCI Gravel World Series standings. (SG)

One of the most versatile riders among elite women in Nannup is Rosa Klöser. The Canyon-SRAM WorldTour road rider competed at the Tour de France Femmes this year, supporting runner-up Kasia Niewiadoma, and framed the road stage race with gravel wins at The Traka 360 and Sea Otter Europe. Her lead into her fourth Gravel World Championships saw her win a climbing-heavy Pyrénées Catalanes Gravel Tour, and outdistance runner-up Nicole Frain by 15 minutes.

She has competed in three Unbound Gravel 200 races and finished fifth or better, with the victory in 2024. This year she earned points on a debut in the invitation-only Life Time Grand Prix. However, she failed to finish Leadville Trail 100 MTB in August, riding in fifth position when she flatted with 14km to go and eight plugs later could not continue. She pulled out of the Grand Prix knowing that she could not compete at other races.

Germany brings a strong squad to Australia, with proven gravel riders Romy Kasper, Nele Laing, Jade Treffeisen and another Unbound Gravel 200 winner, Carolin Schiff, alongside the 30-year-old Canyon rider. If the squad can form an alliance and work for an in-form Klöser, then she has a good chance for redemption ride in Nannup to heal any Grand Prix wounds. (JT)

'Gee' Schreurs has had her most successful season yet in off-road racing in 2026, winning a trio of Gravel Earth Series events for the series overall title. She also rode to a second career win at the Gralloch and took hard-fought podiums at Unbound Gravel 200 and The Traka 360. She has the endurance and power to conquer the Nannup course with more than 3,000 metres of climbing, nearly triple last year's race, but will she be allowed the freedom to do so?

The tall Dutch rider competes on the powerhouse Specialized Off-road squad, and has often supported her teammate Sofia Gomez Villafañe when the two lined up together, notably at The Mid South and Unbound 200 where they went one-two, Schreurs runner-up both times. They switched roles at Lauf Gravel Worlds where Schreurs earned the win and Villafane took fourth.

While Villafañe is the only representative for Argentina on Saturday for elite women, it probably it might be a little tricky for Schreurs to ride for a trade teammate while in Dutch orange. The very capable Schreurs is a threat in her own right among the seven-rider Dutch squad, but the stacked team may be out to give Marianne Vos a second gravel World title. Then again, racing in the Netherlands last year the home team landed 12 riders in the top 20, including Schreurs, and there was no organised support that led Vos and eventual winner Lorena Wiebes catching, and passing a breakaway ride of teammate Shirin Van Anrooij. Look for Schreurs to be at the front of the race in any regard, and land on the podium. (JT)

Look over the podiums of the last three years at the UCI Gravel World Championships and there is one name you will see a lot of, and that's Florian Vermeersch. The UAE Team Emirates-XRG rider hasn't spent a lot of time on the gravel, with road commitments coming first, but he has certainty made his mark when lining up at the rainbow jersey race right from 2023 when he came second on debut. It was a position he then repeated in 2024, continuing a pattern for the rider that had developed on the road of being up there on big target events, like Paris-Roubaix where he came second in 2021, but never quite having the fortune to have his powerful efforts end in a victory celebration.

That, however, all changed in 2025 in the Netherlands with a solo effort of about 20km that left him claiming a world title. That means Vermeersch will line up as both the defending champion and also as the rider who has been the most regular visitor to the elite men's podium at the race, however there is no doubt he'll be facing a different style of challenge this October, with more gravel, more climbing and more travel plus a strong field to contend with when he gets there. "It would be awesome to be the first two-time winner but I'm aware that it’s not going to be easy," acknowledged Vermeersch when his attendance was announced.

However, with the number 1 on his back and two runner-up spots as well he has proven that he is a rider not to be underestimated when he gets a chance to race for his own results. Indeed, he has already visited the lower steps of the podium at Omloop Het Nieuwsblad, E3 Saxo Classic and the Tour of Britain so far this year, and he is bound to do whatever he can to keep his Gravel World Championships podium run rolling too. (SG)

At this point there is only one more result that could add any real lustre to the trophy case and that's the gold medal at the UCI Gravel World Championships.

The Danish rider hasn't had the best experience at the event so far, with a flat tyre and side cut ruining his race. This year, however, the event has been a focus for the second half of the season, with Würtz Schmidt seeing the Australian event as a key opportunity. He certainly has shown what a formidable foe he is this season, and its hard to go past him as a key favourite even in a field with a number of road ring ins.

However, it will be interesting to see where he is on the start grid and whether that works against him, as while his European Championships delivers UCI points, Unbound 200 and The Traka are both outside the UCI domain so they may be high on prestige but count for nothing when it comes to points. Additionally, at The Traka and Unbound Würtz Schmidt benefited from being part of top gravel team, Specialized-Off Road, who took advantage of their strong trio with Keegan Swenson and Matt Beers, but – in theory at least – they will all be racing for their separate countries at the Gravel World Championships. (SG)

It's been three years since Keegan Swenson last competed at the UCI Gravel World Championships, where he finished fifth in Italy. Since then, Cobe Freeburn has been the only US men's elite rider to crack the top 55. Swenson brings strength and swagger to Team USA as he is a dominant force across any off-road race, from six consecutive wins at Leadville Trail 100 MTB to four victories at SBT GRVL, plus a win and three other top 10s at Unbound Gravel 200, all climbing-heavy courses in the US. This past year won his first rainbow stripes in Switzerland as the 2025 UCI Mountain Bike Marathon World Champion.

The first half of 2026 was delayed by an out-of-competition crash where he suffered a fractured pelvis, but he returned to form with podiums at Sea Otter Classic Gravel, Lauf Gravel Worlds, and the win at SBT GRVL. The Utah native was again the top US finisher at MTB Marathon Worlds, but this time seventh. His effort in the Italian Dolomites provided the only UCI points, as he focused on the US-based Life Time Grand Prix events, where he is at the top of the leaderboard and looking for a fourth title in five years.

With a wildcard entry from Team USA, Swenson has confirmed he will take the start in Nannup by squeezing in the travel between rounds of the Grand Prix. Like a few others, he'll have to miss Little Sugar MTB on October 11, but he'll use that as his one throwaway race in the series. The wide roads with 80% mix of dirt, loose rocks and clay combined with relentless climbing of 3,713 metres of elevation gain are similar to US courses, sure to reward an endurance specialist like Swenson. (JT)

Matt Beers lined up at the very first edition of the UCI Gravel World Championships, but like a large proportion of the gravel world that regularly races in the traditional stronghold of the US, he has been absent since. This, however, is an edition that is hard to pass up for a number of the big names, with a course that plays to the strengths of the discipline specialists and a location that makes it harder for the strong road nations to swamp the front of the grid with a large contingent that can effectively control the race. The South African has won Cape Epic four times, finished second at Unbound this year, won Big Sugar, Belgian Waffle Ride California and Lauf Gravel Worlds last year, plus has been on the podium of The Traka the past two years, in the 200 and 360.

Beers is the type of rider who can hold his own on the climbs, push powerfully in a break and also deliver a solid sprint at the end of it, with a good example being his winning effort against Keegan Swenson at the long-running and unofficial Gravel Worlds last year. They are all skills that could be put to good use on the gravel-heavy course from Nannup, which for the UCI Gravel World Series event this year split the field early. (SG)

There were a long list of riders who we went back and forth on for this fifth and final spot in the men's elite contenders list but in the end it was hard to go past Lukas Pöstlberger. The former road professional, with a Giro d'Italia stage win to his name, has really hit his straps on the gravel this year. He has won a UCI Gravel World Series race, The Gralloch, reclaimed his Austrian Champion's title and celebrated on the line of Europe's biggest gravel event, The Traka. The Traka 200 victory was hard to forget, a tight and well played battle to the line, which he charged toward with Braydn Lange (Canyon x DT Swiss All-Terrain Racing) and the Buff BH duo of Martin Stošek and Wout Alleman chasing as well as having MTB legend Nino Schurter not far behind.

That win has offered clear proof of what he is capable of, and he's also made the trip out to Australia early enough that he has a decent amount of time out on the gravel roads around Nannup to explore the course and acclimatise. We saw what happened in Spain earlier this year when he put a clear target on an event and everything runs to plan.

items.title: Charm City Cross Day 2: Manon Bakker and Tofik Beshir sweep weekend with C2 victories on muddy Baltimore course
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
Manon Bakker (Alpe d'Huzes) and Tofik Beshir (CXD Trek Bikes) conquered the mud and won the C2 elite races at Charm City Cross, sweeping both days of UCI races in Baltimore, Maryland. The pair also secured overall titles in the six-race US Cyclocross Series (USCX).

Even with overnight rain and continued drizzle on Sunday on the twisting Druid Hill Park course, Bakker did not make a switch to mud tyres to start the race and used the speed to gain an early advantage. Sidney McGill (Materiaal-Lastig) matched her pace on the first pass of Mansion Hill, but then put a foot down and disconnected from the Dutch rider for the rest of the race. Bakker would solo the rest of the way, despite slipping several times and having to make pit stops, and score her fifth victory in the series.

"These 3 weeks have shown me why I love 'cross so much. The competition during the games and the fun outside. Feels good to be back on track," Bakker posted on Instagram a day later.

McGill, who won the C2 race at Virginia's Blue Ridge Go Cross a week ago, rolled across the muddy finish line in second place, 34 seconds back. Mia Aseltine (Competitive Edge Racing) took third, another 14 seconds later. With fifth place, Aseltine's teammate Kaya Musgrave locked in third overall in the USCX.

Bakker finished second in the series each of the last two seasons, but was nothing but dominant this year, saying "Finally, I got it".

She announced on social media last month that she did not have a team for her cyclo-cross season, so would compete in a blue kit to promote a cancer foundation. "Alpe d'Huzes is a charity that is very close to me, the mountain I've been climbing since I was young. The slogan 'Giving up is not an option' fits me perfectly now," she wrote on Instagram.

In the men's race, it was a showdown between Beshir and Pan American champion Andrew Strohmeyer. Now with Competitive Edge Racing, Strohmeyer took the hole shot and then rode in tandem with his Comp Edge teammate Ryan Drummond. However, on the second lap, Strohmeyer was on his own against the CXD Trek Bikes duo of Beshir and Miles Mattern.

Beshir and Strohmeyer then locked horns for the back half of the race, each trying to find any grip on the slippery course. They tangled with three laps to go in the pits, Strohmeyer hitting the deck, and then again on an off-camber section on the final lap, Beshir taking an outside line that interrupted the momentum of Strohmeyer, who again went down.

“I was trying to hold back a little bit and save energy for the later part of the race,” Strohmeyer said. “The separation came naturally. No one really accelerated. People just make mistakes and the people who stay consistent start riding away.”

The 19-year-old Ethiopian stayed away to the finish, his fifth victory in the series. Tyler Clark (Caledon Hills Cycling Armada) would slot into second place by 18 seconds, while Competitive Edge put Dylan Zakrajsek into the final podium spot, followed by Drummond in fourth and Strohmeyer in fifth. Clark would finish second overall in the USCX, while Calvin Conaway, eighth on Sunday, finished third overall.

"It was definitely hard, but I was just trying to have fun and trying to follow Strohmeyer and learn from him,” Beshir said to organisers. “I saw my opportunity and I chopped him a little bit. I really felt bad because I respect this guy.

"You improve every year that you come here, but you don't really know how much [you’ve improved] until you go out and you do it."

He noted that the wet conditions made the pit stops dangerous. “I immediately regretted it once I came out of the pit and saw he crashed. Yes, it is racing, but I have so much respect for this guy.”

USCX included three consecutive weekends of C1 and C2 races in 2026, with openers at Rochester Cyclocross in New York and the second round at Virginia's Blue Ridge GO Cross in Virginia, both in September. Charm City Cross concluded the series.

items.title: Lidl-Trek and Gaia Realini agree to end contract a year early
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
One season before her current contract was due to expire at the end of 2027, Lidl-Trek and Italian rider Gaia Realini have mutually agreed to part ways at the end of 2026, the German team announced on Monday.

"After four years together - four precious years that have contributed so much to my personal growth and brought so many great emotions - we have decided that the time has come to go our separate ways," said Realini in the announcement.

"Thank you, Lidl-Trek, for everything we have shared and experienced together."

Lidl-Trek signed the diminutive climber in 2023, after she had impressed racing for Continental team Isolmant-Premac-Vittoria, notably at the Giro d'Italia Women. She found immediate success in her first race, taking second on the queen stage and overall at the UAE Tour Women behind teammate at the time and compatriot Elisa Longo Borghini.

From there, Realini only kicked on to become one of the top climbers in the world, taking third at La Flèche Wallonne, seventh at Liège-Bastogne-Liège, and winning Trofeo Oro in Euro in her first spring as a professional.

As the summer of stage racing rolled around, Realini proved to be a revelation, finishing third overall and winning a stage at La Vuelta a Femenina, then matching that GC result of third at the Giro d'Italia Women and Tour de l'Avenir.

This decision was vindicated by her highlight result of fifth overall at her maiden Tour de France Femmes, which she backed up with third on GC at the Tour de Romandie; by this point, Realini was an established GC leader, built for the most vicious, steep climbs.

However, a fractured elbow in training ruined her start to the 2025 season, and she's struggled to return to her previous best ever since, failing to finish in the top 15 of any race she started in her third season on Lidl-Trek.

While still not at her 2023-2024 peak level, Realini has started to find better results in this ongoing season, taking eighth and 12th on the two key climbing stages at the Vuelta, and finishing 10th overall at the Faun Tour Femmes. Her most recent result was 14th at the Giro dell'Emilia Donne, with Tre Valli Varesine the only remaining race on her confirmed schedule for 2026.

Realini is the third confirmed Lidl-Trek women's departure for 2027, with Felicity Wilson-Haffenden joining Fenix-Premier Tech, Shirin van Anrooij heading for Canyon-SRAM, and Amanda Spratt retiring.

Whether Realini will continue in 2027, and where that may be, is yet to be confirmed.

items.title: Noa Isidore sprints to Coppa Bernocchi victory to claim another Italian win for Decathlon CMA CGM
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Noa Isidore (Decathlon CMA CGM) emerged victorious from a messy sprint at the 107th Coppa Bernocchi, taking victory from the bunch with a powerful kick in Legnano ahead of Tommaso Dati (Team UKYO).

The final run to the line was marred by a nasty crash with 700 metres to go, several riders including Ben Swift (Netcompany Ineos) coming down before the sprint was opened up.

As the split bunch ramped up in pace, Dorian Godon (Netcompany Ineos) and Matteo Trentin (Tudor) tried to storm into the slipstream of late attacker Gil Gelders (Soudal-QuickStep), only to be overhauled by those charging quickly behind them.

Isidore speared his way through the middle and past the fast-finishing Dati for the win, with Marijn van den Berg (EF Education EasyPost) taking third on Monday.

"It's a good finish for me. The goal today was to win, so I came here in Italy for that and I'm very happy," said Isidore after the finish, taking his third victory as a professional in his second year on Decathlon's WorldTour squad.

"I'm really happy this year I can be a leader sometimes with my team, and I proved I can win, so I'm happy for me and my teammates who worked for me.

"In the sprint, I just saw the guy from [UKYO], and I thought, 'Just push, push, push, push, you can do it', and I won, so it's good."

Three riders from the early breakaway survived all the way until 1.6k to go, with the charging bunch also bringing back a powerful chasing group that contained Jhonatan Narváez (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) and Neilson Powless (EF Education - EasyPost) inside 10km to go.

It was Samuele Zoccarato (MBH Bank CSB Telecom Fort), Sergio Samitier (Cofidis), and Ben Granger (Solution Tech NIPPO Rali) who had made it into the finale from the break, but even with the Spaniard's undying efforts, they were unable to hold off the chase led mostly by Ineos, EF and Uno-X Mobility.

No team really had full control in the finale, though, which was true of the majority of the action near Milan, leading to several teams accelerating their leaders to the front, which played a role in the crash of Ben Swift and several others.

In fact, the race winner came dangerously close to being involved in the high-speed incident, as the rider who inadvertently caused Swift to lose balance, as he was squeezed by an EF rider, which caused a ripple effect in the bunch and saw more than six riders hit the deck hard next to the pavement.

"I think it's Filippo Ganna next to me," said Isidore, but it was actually Swift, wearing the number four dossard for Ineos, "and the guy from EF just pushed me and I couldn't do anything, so I hope Filippo is good now. But it's like that,"

items.title: 'I've looked at the images hundreds of times' – Giulio Ciccone pleads for transparency as he questions controversial photo finish loss to Evenepoel at European Championships
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
After missing out on the European title by the narrowest of margins, just 0.0028 seconds, Giulio Ciccone (Italy) has pleaded for clarity when it comes to the photo finish that confirmed Remco Evenepoel (Belgium) as the champion from a tight two-up sprint in Slovenia.

Taking to Instagram almost 24 hours after the elite men's road race, the now controversial photo finish was still on Ciccone's mind, after the images showed what looked close to a dead heat, with Evenepoel only snatching the win by a matter of millimetres.

He never questioned that Evenepoel was the strongest rider in the race, but Ciccone struggled to accept the photo finish result without further proof, insisting that he just wanted to "see the photo finish on the real finish line."

"It's hard to control my emotions after yesterday's race. But I want to start from something that is out of the question for me," wrote Ciccone on Monday. "Remco was the strongest rider yesterday. He rode like a champion, he could interpret and manage a complex race and offered an extraordinary performance.

"Then there's the photo finish. The title was awarded with a difference of 0.0028 seconds, i.e. 2.8 thousandths. I've looked at the available images hundreds of times and, in the filming where the finish line is visible, I keep seeing a dynamic that I cannot reconcile with that verdict.

"This morning the commissioners, together with the federal technicians, explained to me how it works and the criteria with which the photo finish was interpreted. So I'm not asking for another explanation.

"I am asking to see the photo finish that corresponds exactly to the actual finish line. I would like to be able to see, unmistakably, the passing of our two wheels at the exact point where, according to the regulations, arrival is determined. Because if a European title is decided by 2.8 thousandths of a second, I think it’s legitimate to ask that that very passage can be shown with the same precision with which the result was determined.

"I'm not asking that a television shot will replace [the] photo finish. I'm not questioning the value of Remco nor the amazing race he ran. I am asking a very simple question: see the photo finish on the real finish line. If that picture confirms the verdict, there is nothing else to add. But until that correspondence is shown to me, for me it remains a question to which I have not yet received an answer."

The UEC, which organises the European Championships, told that they have two photo-finish systems, one on either side of the road, and that images from both of these systems were shown to Ciccone and the Italian federation, along with an explanation of how the technology works.

Ciccone was able to hang onto Evenepoel's accelerations on the final lap, and after mostly sitting on his wheel in the final run to the line, opened up his sprint early around the final corner. He looked as though he had it won, getting the jump on the Belgian, but Evenepoel came back with enough speed to catch him on the line with an elite bike throw.

After a long wait, Evenepoel was announced as the winner, leaving Ciccone banging his handlebars before the frustration turned to disappointment, and he was left hunched over a barrier with his agent, Alex Carera, there to console him.

In cycling, photo finishes are not taken by a regular camera, meaning that questions were raised as soon as the images appeared on screen, with Ciccone's bike appearing smaller than reality in the picture, and Evenepoel's longer.

What's actually happening is that a single vertical strip at the finish line is continuously being scanned every millisecond, resulting in the photo finish, and the X axis being a representation of time – in this case 0.0028 seconds – not of distance.

This is what causes the distortion of both riders and their bikes, as explained by Belgian broadcaster : "The end result looks like a two-dimensional image of a single moment, but in reality, they are photos of lines placed one after another." Italian publication further explained the process, with 15,000 images being produced of the strip in the last second, with Evenepoel arriving first by three millimetres.

Similar photo finish controversy is not unusual in cycling, with Wout van Aert's victory ahead of Tom Pidcock at the Amstel Gold Race in 2021 also raising the same questions. On that occasion, it was just six millimetres in favour of the Belgian that landed him the victory.

items.title: 'In terms of potential he has everything, absolutely everything' – From late call-up to first race with pro team, Matthew Peace looks right at home
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
It was unexpected, but Peace was ready and prepared for what was to come, after all this was a path his older brother Oliver had taken last year, which perhaps gave the 19-year-old confidence to follow his brother into the Picnic PostNL development programme.

But, as he said of this pathway, "knowing what to expect and also doing it is two different things". This was especially true when this late season race was "a bit of a surprise" and there certainly hadn't been time to get set for the conditions, which proved a formidable foe.

"It took me a couple days to get used to the heat and the humidity. It was completely different here because I was just in the UK and it was a bit cooler there," Peace told on the sidelines of the race on stage 6, where even walking to sign-on was enough to work up a sweat.

"I didn't have pressure or expectation coming into the race. It was just learning, so it's just been a really nice experience."

Peace may not have gone into the race with any pressure but he certainly wasn't there to make up numbers, with the plan being that he would support their main GC option Mattia Gaffuri. The Italian, however, had a brutal run at the event, first having to grapple with stomach problems on the first climbing stage on day two and then, when he was starting to feel better, crashing early and finding out afterwards that he had ridden much of the stage with a broken hand.

These days were certainly not ones that followed the plan but Peace was playing his part regardless, finishing 22nd on stage 2 to Gunung Jerai and 13th in the Cameron Highands, while there was than also a 21st in the Genting Highlands.

"I'm quite happy with how it's been going. I've just been like holding on for as long as I can each day, and I seem to be performing quite well. And I was here to support Mattia, and he was hurt. So it was a bit unfortunate we lost him, but then I just did what I could," said Peace, with his efforts not ending in the mountains as there were also digs for the breaks in the later stages.

In the end he finished 19th overall, the youngest rider by far in the top 20. Importantly, it also gave him a one up in the sibling rivalry with his older brother Oliver, who came 42nd overall at the race in 2025, because, he joked, one of his targets was "trying to do better than he [Oliver] did last year".

Even though this was Peace's very first race with the top-tier team, and indeed his first ProTour level race, such are the hopes for the talented British rider that when we spoke to his sports director Melvin Rulliere mid-way through the race, he seemed pleased, and not in the least surprised by the performance of the youngest member of the squad.

"A year ago he was fifth in the World Championship Junior, and we know now how the young kids are ready to race. So he is in a role where he is here to support a leader and learn from from that. But yeah, in terms of potential, he has everything, absolutely everything," Rulliere said.

"For sure, he will be a good rider. Physically, he climbs really well, but also he has a really good aptitude in riding a flat stage."

items.title: Ángel Arroyo, 'a legend of Spanish cycling', dies aged 70
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Ángel Arroyo, the 1983 Tour de France runner-up who is widely credited with sparking a revival in Spanish cycling, died on Sunday at the age of 70.

Tributes have since flooded in from Spain any beyond for a rider whose palmarès might have ended up fairly modest in proportion but who nevertheless is seen as making a much bigger contribution to the sport in Spain and the decades of success that followed his career.

Spain had celebrated Tour de France victories thanks to Federico Bahamontes in 1959 and Luis Ocaña in 1973, but there had been a slump in the years that followed the latter’s success. Arroyo led the line for the Reynolds team when they started as a professional outfit in 1980, and his success was swiftly followed by Pedro Delgado, who won the Tour in 1988, and Miguel Indurain, who won it five times in the 1990s when the squad was known as Banesto.

It’s now known as Movistar, in what is the longest-running team in the sport, and they have just celebrated a Spanish Vuelta a España winner in Enric Mas after years of success thanks to, among others, the former world champion Alejandro Valverde.

Valverde, who now works for the Spanish Cycling Federation, was among those to pay tribute to Arroyo on Monday, writing: “Rest in peace Ángel Arroyo. One of the great names of Spanish cycling in the 1980s.”

The Movistar team added: "Ángel Arroyo has died, a legend of Spanish cycling and one of the great riders of our team. With him, in 1983, we stepped on the podium of the Tour de France for the first time. He was a fabulous rider and one of the best climbers of his time."

As is common in professional cycling, Arroyo’s legacy is a complicated one. He was stripped of the overall title of the 1982 Vuelta a España after testing positive for the banned stimulant methylphenidate. The news came out a few days after Arroyo had celebrated what appeared to be a breakthrough achievement. Arroyo didn't deny the offense but described the use of such substances as widespread and has described himself as the 'moral winner' of the race.

In any case, Arroyo went on to make the podium of the Tour de France the following year, finishing runner-up behind the young Laurent Fignon. He did so after taking his most famous victory on the stage 15 time trial up the Puy de Dome volcano. The following year, he won the brutal mountain stage into Morzine and finished in sixth place overall.

"They were the seasons in which Spanish cycling recovered its pride and understood that it could once again compete with the French, Belgians, and Italians in the biggest races," writes Nacho Labarga in Monday’s edition of the Spanish newspaper .

"Arroyo was the link that connected two eras: that of the drought years and the generation that would go on to turn the Tour de France into familiar territory for Spanish cycling."

Arroyo’s success waned in the following years, and he retired in 1989 at the age of 32, but not before he’d been part of the Reynolds team that delivered Pedro Delgado to Tour de France glory in 1988.

"He was a cornerstone in building up cycling in our country," Delgado wrote back then.

Arroyo’s legacy is further underlined by the cycling club that was created in his name by his neighbor, Victor Sastre, which gave rise to the likes of José María Jiménez, Pablo Lastras, and a certain Carlos Sastre – Victor’s son and the winner of the 2006 Tour de France.

After retiring from professional cycling, Arroyo, who had little in the way of savings, went on to run a carwash business for many years. "I’m at the age to retire, but I cannot do so," he said in an interview with in 2023. "If I stop, I wouldn’t be able to pay for heating in the winter or air conditioning in the summer. I live hand to mouth."

"Some might see my work as a humiliation, but for me it is not. I like it and I enjoy what I do. I have the life of any other worker.”

items.title: 'Perhaps it will wear off and I will go back to suffering' – World Champion Brandon McNulty still riding high as he makes impressive start to rainbow jersey reign
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Brandon McNulty opened up his time as World Champion this past weekend in Italy with two impressive races at the Giro dell'Emilia and Coppa Agostoni, where he was 10th and second, respectively, but also on the immediate attack in his new rainbow jersey.

He, of course, started as one of the heavy favourites for the former, and did light up the decisive San Luca climb on the third of five ascents, but McNulty was unable to go with the winning move led by Visma-Lease a Bike's Matteo Jorgenson and eventual winner Davide Piganzoli, who played things perfectly in the finale.

As for reasons for not being at your best, though, none can be better than the one McNulty gave on his Instagram, detailing how the superhuman 35km solo effort – which so nearly came unstuck – he put in to claim the rainbow jersey in Montreal was still taking its toll.

"I enjoyed every single second of my first race in rainbows today," said McNulty. "It’s safe to say I left every single bit of my legs, and probably some pieces of my soul on roads last weekend so I’m still missing a bit, but there’s still a lot of opportunities to come!"

That next opportunity came on the subsequent afternoon in Lissone, and after his UAE team did much of the early work, McNulty found himself off the front in the eventual race-winning move of seven riders with 40km to go.

Six made it into the final sprint after no one was able to get away solo, leaving McNulty to try and get his first win in rainbows from a small group kick. His punch was solid, but not enough to come around Frenchman Paul Lapeira (Decathlon CMA CGM), ending his first weekend as World Champion with a second place.

Still riding the wave of what will become a career-defining victory, McNulty has begun his year-long reign with two impressive performances. Yes, when Tadej Pogačar returns next season and they race together, the US rider will still play second fiddle as a super domestique, but that win in Canada could yet propel him to new heights.

"For sure it is still settling in, with the jersey and everything. [Sunday] was good, I am still a bit fatigued from last week and also [on Saturday] I went super hard. It was a really hard race and I was happy to be there in the final, and then sprints can go one way or the other, so I am happy with the efforts today," said McNulty on UAE's team website.

"It is super special [being the World Champion]. I feel like the races pass faster, I don’t really think about kilometres to go anymore. Hopefully that continues! Perhaps it will wear off and I will go back to suffering, but the last two days have been so special. Everybody has been very supportive and I have had so many people come up to me to congratulate me, so I want to say thank you to everybody."

McNulty will next be in action at Tuesday's Tre Valli Varesine, again taking on the role of leader in Pogačar's absence at these Italian Autumn Classics, before he will likely do the same at the final Monument of the 2026 season on Sunday: Il Lombardia.

items.title: 'The last jersey I still wanted and needed' – Champion of championships Remco Evenepoel completes the set with eighth elite title out of eight
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Remco Evenepoel is undeniably one of the greatest riders of this ongoing generation, but as he added the UEC European Championships road race title to his already illustrious palmarès in Slovenia, the Belgian completed the set of winning all eight championship titles available to him.

Across the two disciplines of the road race and individual time trial, at just 26, Evenepoel has now won both at the Belgian National Championships, European Championships, World Championships, and the Olympic Games, in a run spanning back seven years, with 24 medals won at the elite level.

In an era mostly dominated by one rider, Tadej Pogačar, Evenepoel's talents as a time trial expert and elite one-day racer, long known since he burst onto the scene as a junior, have seen him go on to achieve a level of completion the Slovenian has only managed half of.

And looking back to 2018, just 18 months after he had become a cyclist, is it any real surprise? At the Europeans Championships, he did the double in the junior road race and time trial in Zlín, Czechia, before netting an unprecedented double double as he achieved the same feat at the World Championships in Innsbruck, winning both junior rainbow jerseys by more than 1:20.

Even as an inexperienced teenager, Evenepoel was the master of championships, and this latest feat and completion of the championship bingo only adds to his legacy as a rider for the big occasion.

"This jersey is added to my list of achievements, but you played a big part in that. A huge thank you for that," he added that evening, in his speech to the Belgian team and staff. "The same goes for the staff. Everything was well organised again. Thanks to everyone who contributed even a little bit.

"And I think I'm not riding championships anymore now, right?" he joked. "No, that's not true."

His first major elite title came at the Europeans a year after his junior dominance, vindicating his early step up to the professional level as he beat specialists Kasper Asgreen, Edoardo Affini, Stefan Küng, Alex Dowsett and Filippo Ganna to the title in Alkmaar at just 19.

Evenepoel's next gold medal came at the Belgian Championships, but not until 2022, with his major crash at Il Lombardia in 2020 stunting some of his inevitable progress. He beat then-teammate Yves Lampaert convincingly to the time trial title in Gavere.

Fast forward three months and Evenepoel became road race World Champion in Wollongong, claiming the rainbow jersey by more than two minutes after he went solo in the last 25km.

In 2023, he added two more major titles, winning the Belgian national road race title ahead of Alec Segaert in Izegem, before going on to win the first of his four World titles in the elite time trial, scorching to victory in Stirling after finishing on the podium in his first three attempts.

He made history a season later, becoming the first male rider to do the double at the Olympic Games in Paris, dominating the race against the clock, before claiming an iconic solo win in the road race. With the help of Wout van Aert marking Mathieu van der Poel up the Montmartre climb, Evenepoel was able to time his attack to perfection, surviving despite a late bike change, and celebrating in front of the Eiffel Tower.

With this feat achieved, Evenepoel's tally of championship wins was already at seven, with just the European road race remaining on his hit list. Before the race in Ljubljana, Evenepoel had gone close twice to completing the eight, losing out to Sonny Colbrelli in a two-up sprint in Trento in 2021, and only being beaten by Pogačar in France a season ago.

Lining up at the start with Pogačar still out injured, Evenepoel was the heavy favourite to claim the iconic European jersey, but as is typical of the Belgians' entire career, it was never going to be as simple as him riding off solo into the sunset.

The Italian team mounted a major challenge, upping the pace for their big leaders Giulio Ciccone and Christian Scaroni, and just as the race started to really heat up and Evenepoel began his move on the Možjanca climb, with Ciccone following him, the Belgian crashed.

A week after the disappointment of failing to deliver at the World Championships, Evenepoel's hope of the eighth was looking like it might go up in smoke, but with luck on his side, his bike wasn't badly broken, and his teammates were just coming up to help dig him out of the hole.

Maxim van Gils and Ramses Debruyne brought him back to the front, and the next time up, he was able to put the hammer down again. But still, the race wasn't done, with Ciccone able to follow and then staying – for the vast majority of the run for home – in the stronger rider's wheel.

Not only did it take a two-up sprint to decide the day, but one of the closest photo finishes in recent memory confirmed Evenepoel was the champion, narrowly pipping Ciccone with an expert bike throw by the barest of margins in Šenčur. Not only did he complete the set, but Evenepoel had righted the wrongs of Montreal.

"I might not have really shown it, but I was still very disappointed in myself and my performance. I also felt like I had disappointed the whole country with my performance," he said. "I still hope that everyone is proud now that we are back. And sorry again for last week's World Championship. Now I'm going to celebrate this one big time."

Evenepoel travelled back to Belgium today, but will be on the road once again on Wednesday, "Because there is another important race on Saturday," as he heads for Italy to take on Il Lombardia. Second in the past two seasons behind Pogačar, Evenepoel will be the favourite for the Monument and will look to close out a successful 2026 season with a bang.

items.title: Visma-Lease a Bike promote former rider Nathan Van Hooydonck to new leading sporting director role
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Visma-Lease a Bike have announced that Nathan Van Hooydonck has been promoted to a new role as sporting director.

Van Hooydonck, whose last race came at the 2023 Tour of Britain, initially transitioned to work as a VIP guest guide during major races throughout the season. In October 2024, he took up the commercial role, and now, he steps up to a position as leader of Visma's Sport Management Team (SMT).

"Nathan is still young, but incredibly eager to learn and someone who feels completely connected to this team and to what we want to achieve together," said Visma-Lease a Bike CEO Richard Plugge.

"He not only knows our culture, he acts according to it and embodies it. For years, I have also seen how determined he is to win and how much it means to him when we do not. As a former rider, he also has the credibility to have an opinion on the sport and to express it.

"Through his experience within the Business Team, he has quickly learned to look beyond the sporting side of things and to see the connection with the rest of our organisation.

"That gives us confidence that he will do a very good job in this role. And he certainly will not be doing it alone. With people such as Mathieu Heijboer, who has been and will continue to be an important part of our organisation, Nathan can draw on a great deal of knowledge and experience."

Visma say that Van Hooydonck will take responsibility for "defining and overseeing the team's key sporting objectives." Van Hooydonck, who turns 31 next week, will also "safeguard the long-term vision, values and culture" of the team.

Van Hooydonck joins Plugge, Marc Reef, Mathieu Heijboer, Robbert de Groot, and Patrick Broe on Visma's SMT. As part of the setup, he'll be partly responsible for ensuring the squad can continue to challenge and beat bigger budget squads, including UAE Team Emirates-XRG.

He said that his time spent on the commercial side of Visma allowed him to see the team "from a different perspective."

"It has helped me to better understand the organisation and experience how all the different parts are connected. Richard has also played a huge role in my development and in giving me the opportunity I now have to take on this role within the team," said Van Hooydonck.

"Ultimately, for me, it comes down to one thing: winning. To achieve that, we need to move in the same direction as an organisation every single day. That means being willing to challenge each other, to push each other and, at the same time, to make sure everyone feels involved in what we are trying to achieve together. I am really looking forward to contributing to that from this role."

Van Hooydonck isn't the first change at Visma for the 2027 season. So far, the men's team has brought on board neo-pro Matisse Van Kerckhove and Mark Donovan (Pinarello-Q36.5), while the women's squad will welcome Femke Markus (SD Worx-Protime) and Maike van der Duijn (Canyon-SRAM).

On the staff side, head of the sport management team Jacco Verhaeren is on the outgoing list, with the team having announced his departure "decided in consultation with the team" back in September. After the surprise departure of head of racing Grischa Niermann, announced back in June, Reef stepped up into that role on September 1 and will carry that into 2027.

items.title: Can anyone challenge world champion Marlen Reusser? – European Championship elite women's time trial contenders
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
The European Championships have only included elite races since 2016, and in those 10 editions just four riders have held the women's time trial title, with Ellen van Dijk, Marlen Reusser, Anna van der Breggen and Lotte Kopecky all tasting success. Will there be a new name in 2026? Or will Marlen Reusser set a new record of five titles, to go with her second world title won in Montreal two weeks ago?

This year’s race starts and finishes in the central Slovenian town of Šenčur, and whoever takes the title this year will need to overcome a challenging 22.1km course which includes almost 400m of vertical ascent, almost all of which comes in the first half of the race.

The main challenge comes in the form of the climb to Možjanca, which averages 10.2% gradient over its 2km and tops out a third of the way through the course. Though there are steeper ramps at the top, it’s a fairly steady gradient which will suit the TT specialists who can set a strong rhythm.

While there are narrow sections and some turns, it is not a technical route, though there is a tight hairpin turn on the descent where the road surface appears fairly poor, so riders will need to be concentrated to get through that unscathed. After that, the final kilometres are almost entirely flat, and while it’s a different type of course, it’s hard to look past those who performed well at the Montreal World Championships. Here are our contenders for the stars and stripes skinsuit.

After her dominant ride at the World Championships in Montreal, Switzerland’s Marlen Reusser will start as the outright favourite for another title. While her palmarès indicates she is far more than a pure time trial specialist, she is currently the most accomplished woman against the clock and bang in form, finishing third in the Euros road race over the weekend.

What’s more, the course suits her, though others may be better than her on the early steep climb, once over that, expect the Swiss superstar to build her advantage.

The one note of caution is her performance on the mountain time trial of this year’s Giro d’Italia Women when she finished well behind winner, Anna van der Breggen, though the Dutchwoman is absent from this year's European Championships.

Maybe another motivation for Reusser is her place in history. Should she take a fifth title on Wednesday, she will hold the record for European titles, surpassing Ellen van Dijk’s four victories, which she equalled last year.

Winning the Euros road race on Saturday, Demi Vollering might be the best all-round rider in the women’s peloton at the moment, but she’s not won a time trial since the 2024 Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift, and only managed eighth place in the recent World Championships.

The Slovenian course suits her more than that in Canada, though, the steep, early climb will almost certainly allow her to gain time on all her rivals, though she will then need to hold on to her advantage for the rest of the course.

She might not be a regular winner against the clock, but she is almost always there or thereabouts and clearly in form right now, winning both Worlds and Europeans road races. Combine that ability with a course which suits her and a voracious appetite for success, and no one would be surprised if she takes another victory on Wednesday.

After finishing just outside the medals in the Montreal individual time trial, Elisa Longo Borghini won the mixed team relay before taking third in the road race, so it’s clear the Italian has struck a rich vein of form.

After missing much of the spring with illness, she has been improving since returning to health, and we should expect her to make the podium on Wednesday. Longo Borghini is arguably a better climber than Reusser, and she’s certainly a better descender, so if she can take time on the Swiss rider on the climb, she should be able to consolidate that on the descent.

However, in contrast to the prolific Reusser, she has only ever won two time trials outside the Italian Championships, the most recent of which was two years ago, 10 years after the other. However, like Vollering she is always there or thereabouts, and a top result is likely.

Fifth in Montreal, Cédrine Kerbaol is another rider in fine form to take on Europeans this week. At 25-years-old she is still improving every year and, as one of the peloton’s preeminent climbers we can expect her to deal with the early gradients well.

Like Longo Borghini, she’s also a brilliant descender, so may well be able to take time on the descent, and her performance in Canada is proof she can deal with the flat run-in well enough to make the podium.

Though she was only the second-best German rider in the World Championships last week, taking seventh place, just over a minute behind compatriot Franziska Koch, Antonia Niedermaier is by far the better climber of the pair and will be able to gain time in those challenging early kilometres.

The 23-year-old took fourth place in the Giro d’Italia’s mountain time trial in May, just 15 seconds behind Reusser, and though this is less challenging terrain than that, Niedermaier can be expected to put in a good performance in Slovenia this week.

While she may not be the climber her compatriot Niedermaier is, Franziska Koch has proved this year that there is almost nothing she cannot do. Since arriving at FDJ United-Suez she has improved exponentially, and her TT bronze medal in Montreal shows just how good she is against the clock.

While her climbing is much better than before, the day’s ascent will prove a major obstacle to success for Koch, though there is every chance she can make up time on the descent and flatter parts of the course.

This year’s Polish time trial champion, Dominika Włodarczyk, is much improved against the clock this season, with her ninth place at the Worlds a best-ever result. Only 25, she has always been good at the discipline, bagging some decent results as a junior, it’s just taken her time to become competitive in the elite ranks.

What’s more, she has established herself as an excellent climber, finishing eighth on the Mont Ventoux stage of the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift this year and finishing seventh overall, so the Možjanca climb will be well within her talents.

Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney will also race the TT for Poland, and whilst the time trial was once considered one of her weaknesses, she put in a hugely improved ride against the clock at the Tour de France earlier this summer, so don't write her off entirely.

  • Juliette Berthet (France) – Will look to come back from an unusually sub-par performance at Worlds
  • –reat against the clock but unlikely to challenge the very best for a medal
  • Lauren Dickson (Great Britain) – Sixth on the Giro mountain TT, but still developing as a time trialist

items.title: UAE Team L'IMAD shutter development squad amid ongoing turbulence
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
UAE Team L'IMAD are closing their development squad at end of 2026, they announced on Monday, but they have vowed to continue supporting the riders through 2027.

The UAE Development Team was set up in 2023 as a women's Continental team, and has seen riders like Paula Blasi, Lara Gillespie and Linda Zanetti pass through its ranks, all of whom are now successful WorldTour riders.

However, despite taking multiple wins in 2026, the separate development programme will soon be closing down, with the team integrating its development mission into the WorldTour team. This year, the UAE Development Team has 11 riders on its roster, though only one – Abigail Miller – officially had a contract for 2027.

"UAE Team L’IMAD has confirmed that the UAE Development Team will not continue as a separate UCI Women’s Continental Team for the 2027 season. Following a review of its sporting organisation, the team is changing how it supports the development of young riders," a statement from the team read.

"Within its WorldTour structure, UAE Team L’IMAD will continue to develop young riders who are ready to take that step. They will have the opportunity to learn alongside experienced teammates, with their progression guided by individual readiness and racing opportunities suited to their development."

The statement also stated that the current riders will continue to be supported by the team in 2027 "with support tailored to their individual needs and stage of development", adding that "the priority is to help each athlete continue progressing in her career".

With 11 riders on the team this year, though, it's unclear what that support will look like – not all of them can be promoted to the WorldTour team, so the majority of riders will have to find a new team if they wish to continue racing on the road in 2027, even with UAE support.

The landscape of women's development teams

Whilst almost all men's WorldTour teams now have U23 development squads, it is still a rarer concept in women's cycling, where there is no dedicated U23 racing circuit. In 2026, AG Insurance-Soudal, Canyon-SRAM, Liv AlUla Jayco, UAE and Fenix-Premier Tech all have development teams, but that list will drop to just four in 2027.

Whilst plenty of teams opt to integrate their development efforts within their main WorldTour squad, or by partnering with an existing Continental team, the benefit of having a specific development squad is that it gives teams many more roster spots for young riders, and the ability to run a dual programme.

Despite losing those extra spots, and therefore unavoidably narrowing the scope of their development programme, UAE affirmed that helping riders progress is still a core part of the team's ethos.

"We are proud of what our Development Team has achieved and grateful to everyone who has contributed. Our priority now is to support our riders through this change and help them continue progressing," team president Melissa Moncada said.

"Developing young talent remains part of our commitment to women’s cycling. We want every young rider in our WorldTour team to have the time, guidance and opportunities she needs to grow.”

Turbulent times at UAE Team L'IMAD

The closure of UAE's development team is not only unfortunate news for their current roster and the women's development circuit in general, but it is also another big change in what has been a turbulent summer for UAE Team L'IMAD.

They are going through a significant management restructuring, with team CEO Yana Seel exiting the team in August, and no permanent replacement in post yet. Senior DS Cherie Pridham was touted as a possible successor, but the Brit is also leaving the team for Human Powered Health, along with multiple other sports directors – over half the current DS line-up is departing at the end of 2026.

Sponsored by a UAE sovereign wealth fund and widely understood to have one of the largest budgets in the women's peloton, money does not seem to be the issue at UAE Team L'IMAD, but rather questions and concerns over management and stability behind the scenes.

At WorldTour level, the team has made two new signings for 2027 so far – Pfeiffer Georgi from Picnic PostNL and Lily Williams from Human Powered Health – and will still have riders like Elisa Longo Borghini and Mavi García on their books next season, so there is no question over their survival or strength, just the shape and future of the management behind the team.

items.title: Most aero socks are a waste of money: Here's the wind tunnel verified proof
items.author: josh.croxton@futurenet.com (Josh Croxton)
items.content:
Even though aerodynamics has become priority number one for most competitive cyclists buying new kit, aero socks are perhaps the most ridiculed upgrade of the past decade.

Speaking generally, the promise of 'free' (albeit often very expensive) speed is hard to ignore, compounded by the fact that pro cyclists – who rarely need to worry about the accompanying expense – place extreme importance on the matter as their careers can be made or lost by it.

Yet while most aero products are embraced quickly and without second thought, aero socks took a good while to gain acceptance. They didn't pass the fashion test, and the old guard dismissed them as a gimmick or a marginal gain too far. But when comparative tests started showing measurable benefits, more and more teams started wearing them, and nowadays, they're a staple in the pro peloton. You'll spot amateurs in them too, especially on race day.

We've now hit a point where some aero socks are so highly technical and researched that they regularly fetch up to £50+ per pair, and some even stretch as far as £100, and that's before we get into custom territory. The thing is, others can be had for just £3 if you know where to shop.

So do you actually stand to save more watts by buying the more expensive - or name brand - socks?

To find out, we collated 26 pairs of socks and headed to the wind tunnel.

Our cohort included 22 pairs from named cycling brands, including Velotoze, Rule28, Aero Cycling Gear, NoPinz, Rapha, Castelli, Assos and more.

It also included a pair of comparatively cheap 'Rock Bros' socks that we bought from Amazon, an extremely cheap pair of 'West Biking' socks from Temu, a pair of cotton everyday socks from the British high-street clothing store Next, as well as some technical hiking socks from another high-street store.

The full list, in alphabetical order, is as follows:

  • Aero Cycling gear v5 Hexaflow
  • Mountain Warehouse Hiking Socks
  • Next everyday cotton socks
  • Rule 28 Neo Aero Sock (Double Layer)

So are expensive aero socks any faster than cheap aero socks? Does a pair of aero socks beat a pair of nominally 'standard' cycling socks? What about compared to a pair of everyday or hiking socks?

The title of this article has probably already given you a clue as to the answers to some of these questions, but scroll down to find out the details.

Unlike previous CN Labs tests, where you're forced to read through (or scroll past) 3000 words explaining the protocols, caveats and standardisations, I'm going to dive straight into the results and do the nerdy stuff later. Please do take time to read the nerdy bits below, though, as that'll help you understand how we landed on the data and what caveats apply.

It's also important to state up front that the data is subject to an error margin of 0.2w at the lower speed, and 1.17w at the higher speed.

The biggest thing of note here is that there are very small differences between all the pairs of aero socks on test. There's just 1.85 watts between the fastest and slowest, and the difference between many of the socks in between is smaller than our error margin.

The Aero Cycling Gear V5 was fastest, but both NoPinz's Sonic and Rule 28's One Aero Sock can lay claim to victory too, with the error margin taken into account.

According to Rule 28, its more expensive Neo Aero Sock, with its double-layer finish, was designed for speeds over 55km/h for time trialling and track riding, so its mid-table result isn't a surprise here. It's also a lesson in choosing the right product for your needs, as spending more money doesn't automatically equal better performance across the board.

Just off the podium, the NoPinz Hypersonic Mk2, Sockeloen FSOTP 468 and Santini Madss are close behind, with Castelli's Fast Feet 4 sitting just behind those.

And then the next dozen are all pretty much indistinguishable, despite the price bracket ranging from £3.68 for the 'West Biking' brand of socks we bought from Temu, to £50 for the Rapha and Assos options.

Behind this, there are small steps down, before a bigger jump to the two pairs of non-cycling socks.

The error margin here is around 50% bigger than that of the 30km/h test, meaning even more potential for crossover between results. The results show that the Rule 28 One Aero Sock banked the best result, but it was a bit of a lottery as to which actually came out on top. Any of the top 17 - yes, seventeen - can claim the top spot, because they were all within 1.17 watts (our error margin) of the winner.

And to clarify, this is a pretty tight error margin at such a high speed, just ten counts (or 0.0010) in terms of CdA. So while it looks like we've just performed a bad test that shows all socks as being about the same, that's because all the socks are… about the same.

When you get into the bottom third of the table, we do start to see some differences, but most of those still sit within the error margin of five places either above or below.

Notably, the Velotoze Aero Pro is a step behind the others, despite being a high-priced aero product. Having shared the data with Velotoze, we're at a loss as to what caused this. It could be that the material was overstretched when fitted, or it could have been a glitch. It doesn't concur with Velotoze's own data, which showed them to be 6 watts faster than Velotoze' baseline coolmax socks at 40km/h in its own internal testing.

And the Veto 1.0 is a standard cycling sock by design, with none of your typical aero fabrics or trip strips, nor the common papery thin fragility, but the brand does claim to have tested them in a wind tunnel with good results.

We're looking at a gap of 4.9 watts (+/- 1.17w) between the fastest and slowest cycling socks on test, which is still better than a kick in the teeth, but given the £14.99 pair of Rock Bros socks from Amazon are just as fast as the £30-50 pairs from all the big brands, it's a damning outcome for anyone charging big money promising aero gains.

And like the 30km/h data above, the distant duo at the bottom of the table (in the form of the hiking socks and the everyday cotton socks) are the exception that proves the rule. There's a further five watts between the slowest aero socks and the slowest non-cycling socks.

I guess my main regret here is not taking more 'normal' cycling socks along to see how they compare, but I'm quite confident they'd sit within the error margin too.

While there's no clear trend that we can see, it's interesting to see how the order differs at the two speeds.

The consistent position of the two non-cycling socks – the hiking socks and the cotton everyday socks – at the bottom of the table is reassurance that the wind tunnel was spitting out accurate numbers. If a pair of woolly socks from my local hiking store outperformed dedicated aero socks, I'd be concerned we'd done something wrong.

While it's fair to say the difference between each pair of socks is minimal, can we at least spot a trend with taller generally being faster than shorter?

That's long been the general train of thought. It's why we see time triallists in knee-high socks, and partly why the UCI banned socks over a certain height (although that was mainly because they look weird too).

To find out, I've grouped the socks by their height to see if taller does indeed equal faster.

There's a slight bias towards better performance at the taller heights, but it's far from clearcut. We had socks here ranging from 20cm to 26cm tall, but some of the socks in the 20cm category are just as fast as those up at 24 and 26cm.

This one's so clear-cut that it doesn't even need a graph to prove it. The £3 socks are mid-table, the £14.99 socks are on the podium, and more than one near-£50 pair sits in the bottom third of our test.

There's no clear correlation between price and aerodynamic performance.

On the day, we decided that next time, we'd try to work with a brand like Sockeloen or Vorteq to create a custom-fitted pair to see if that makes any difference. Sockeloen offers a €1000 option that involves aero consultancy, for example.

Of course, cheaper items - socks and otherwise - could cut corners in other areas. They might be faster in a one-minute wind tunnel test, but if they lose their stick and fall down halfway through a ride, or if they lose their stretch and become baggy after three washes, or they fall apart entirely, you're giving away all the aero gains and more.

The contrary to that, though, is that many aero socks from big-name brands are incredibly fragile. Some are much better than others, but the papery finish you get on some is easy to damage. I've ripped three pairs in the past year alone. And the lack of stretch in the material on others means you really need to fight to get them on, which in turn increases the risk of damage.

That's not the subject of today's test, so we will be putting the various socks through their real-world paces to see how they fare in longer-term use.

But even so, when there's no aero performance guarantee, and the risk of damage means they could last just as long as something made less well, why buy something at 3x - or, in the case of the Temu socks, 14x - the price?

There are clearly watts to be saved between the non-cycling socks (everyday cotton and the hiking socks) and the cycling socks, of which the best example is the Veto 1.0.

There is then another small uptick to the nominally 'aero' socks, but the difference between that Veto 1.0 and an 'aero' cycling sock could range anywhere from negative three watts (ie, worse) to a maximum of around six watts (both at 45km/h).

But given our data shows small differences between the aero socks, there's no single winner in today's test. Rule 28 will enjoy the results of the 45km/h test, and likewise Aero Cycling Gear in the 30km/h test, but the reality is the socks are all so close to one another that you, as a consumer, should probably just buy the cheapest, or the ones you like the look of most.

At £3.68, the 'West Biking' socks I bought from Temu promise incredible aero performance in terms of watts saved vs money spent. They did feel pretty basic in their materials, though, as can be expected at a price that would allow you to buy FOURTEEN pairs for the same cost as the most expensive on test.

The feel and quality of the £14.99 'Rock Bros Grid' socks from Amazon were just as good as most of the 'big brand' products, though, so I'd be very tempted to buy those; and that's still between half and a third of the price of most others here. The only downside to those is the big 'Rock' on one leg and 'Bros' on the other, but they make them in dozens of various colours and designs. If they made them in pure white, I expect they'd sell incredibly well.

Assuming you do want to buy something that promises to be aero, there's very little way to know which is the best one for you.

There's no obvious correlation between aero performance and cuff height, price, or brand. They're also all designed to work at varying speeds, and the optimal pair for you will probably depend on what sort of riding you're doing, whether it's windy, how many people you're riding with, and the shape and size of your legs.

Therefore, unless you're going to hire a wind tunnel and a team of data scientists to run simulations on your upcoming race, you're probably best off just buying the cheap ones and spending the rest of the money on carbs.
